title: Change Creates Opportunity. It Also Sucks.
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham revisits her ten-year-old essay 'Give Away Your Legos' and asks how it holds up in the age of AI. Her core claim is that the original message was never about rapid scale but about change: gripping the old responsibilities that built your identity does not stop the world from moving. She adds that you can believe in the opportunity and still hate the change, that grieving is not resisting, and that leaders should literally hold a funeral for what is ending. Because nearly everyone is a beginner with AI, she urges people not to assume they are behind. Her biggest revision is that handing work to AI differs from handing it to humans, since you still own the oversight and cognitive load, and there are things such as judgment, taste, accountability and trust she is now reluctant to outsource.
points: The Legos principle is about change in general, so people who built an identity around a skill should expect to let it evolve rather than defend it.
Leaders should make room for honest grief about what is ending, because forcing excitement tends to bury feelings that resurface later.
Assume your profession survives but looks very different, then ask what you want it to become and how you can help shape that version.
Delegating to AI keeps you accountable for context, review and correction, which adds cognitive load and helps explain why people feel exhausted.
Keep judgment, taste, accountability, relationships and vision in human hands, and ask what AI can help you become better at rather than only what it can do instead of you.
quotes: The problem is that holding on doesn’t stop the change. It just makes it harder to adapt.
You can believe in the opportunity and still hate the change.
Grieving the old thing isn’t the same as resisting the new one.
Throw the funeral. Be sad. Be pissed. Talk about what you loved about the old thing. Work grief is important.
Manoush asked: What would you do if you believed your job was always going to exist, it was just going to look completely different every six years?
the distance from beginner to expert in AI is shockingly small. You are probably not as far behind as you think you are.
You still own the cognitive load for the agents and workflows that you parent. This is part of why I think people are so exhausted.
AI can dramatically increase how much we can produce without necessarily increasing how much we can actually hold in our heads.
There’s another question I find much more interesting: What can AI help me become much better at?
